segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: This conversation with Hilda Carlson Ruberg and Helena Cartwright Carlson, sisters-in-law, took place on June 19, 1976. The interviewer was Karen Purtee.

segments.speaker: Hilda Carlson Ruberg or Helena Carlson
segments.words: Is that a new one?

segments.speaker: Karen Purtee
segments.words: There we go. No, that's the one I used to do. That one you had it for?

segments.speaker: Hilda Carlson Ruberg or Helena Carlson
segments.words: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Karen Purtee
segments.words: Well, I think I had it on the floor, so you didn't have to look at it.

segments.speaker: Hilda Carlson Ruberg or Helena Carlson
segments.words: That was it.

segments.speaker: Karen Purtee
segments.words: Oh, no, I had the black one then. The one that belongs to the museum. I thought you had the black one. Okay, now, we'll start with your family, and then maybe how you got here, or why.

segments.speaker: Hilda Carlson Ruberg or Helena Carlson
segments.words: Yeah, well, my father had been out here during the summer, and he bought this farm out here in Big Meadow. And then in November, I brought the whole family out. There were 11 children at that time. And we landed in Troy on November the 12th. No, November, what was it, November… august… huh… it was on August. No, it was November. November, was it November? November, 1912. And so when we got here, it was at night, and we had to stay in a hotel down here. And in the morning, we got somebody to take us out in a hack, you know, and the mud was hub deep in the streets in Troy. Ooh. And they drove out there. It was three miles out there. And then my brother had come out first. He came out with a carload of stock, you know, horses and cattle and so on. So he was already out there. I see. And so I didn't know from then on. And the house that we moved into was just nothing but these up and down boards with the slabs on the cracks, see. Oh. They had to fix up the house for winter. They relined the house inside, you know, and papered it and slided it on the outside so we could keep warm during the winter. And so then in January, I and my two sisters went to Spokane to find work, you know, because we were a large family. We couldn't go home.

segments.speaker: Karen Purtee
segments.words: And so we were there about... You were about 19 then?

segments.speaker: Hilda Carlson Ruberg or Helena Carlson
segments.words: And we did housework just like everybody else around here went to Spokane to do housework, you know, in those days. You could always get it. And we were there about a year and a half when I married. And then we moved down to Troy, bought a farm up in Burnt Ridge and lived out in Burnt Ridge. Well, up until 48, but then I lost my first husband in 39 and remarried again in, no, in 31, and I remarried again in 36. So I still lived out on the ridge. And then we sold out in 48. Oh.

segments.speaker: Karen Purtee
segments.words: Well, your husband wasn't from Troy then?

segments.speaker: Hilda Carlson Ruberg or Helena Carlson
segments.words: Yeah, well, not the first husband, but he had relatives. Troy. I met him in Spokane. At that time, I didn't know he had relatives at Troy. Oh. The Calberts, you know, like Mrs. Ernest Anderson and Oscar Calbert, and those were his cousins.

segments.speaker: Karen Purtee
segments.words: Oh, small world. Yes, there I was. And then from the... Well, you came from Dakota?

segments.speaker: Hilda Carlson Ruberg or Helena Carlson
segments.words: Hope, North Dakota. Hope, North Dakota. Yeah.

segments.speaker: Karen Purtee
segments.words: And by train?

segments.speaker: Hilda Carlson Ruberg or Helena Carlson
segments.words: By train. And it was, I think, a two and a half day trip out on the train.

segments.speaker: Karen Purtee
segments.words: That seems like a long time for a big family. Were you the oldest girl then?

segments.speaker: Hilda Carlson Ruberg or Helena Carlson
segments.words: I was the oldest girl, yeah. Ed was older than I was, so. But I was the oldest girl. So, I don't know, and then of course they had the farm, you know, and just like anybody else out here, you know. And woods… they cut wood… yeah, well, Ira never did cut any wood, you know. You mean out there on the farm out there? Oh, yeah, the folks out there, yeah. Uh-huh, yeah. They cut wood to make their living, you know, in all of the towns. Oh. So, it was just a farm with just a few acres cleared, you know, and that didn't take very long, so they had several acres, maybe a hundred acres cleared that they were.

segments.speaker: Karen Purtee
segments.words: Now, the boys did this?

segments.speaker: Hilda Carlson Ruberg or Helena Carlson
segments.words: Yeah, my dad and Ed and the other boys, you know. And of course, after they got land enough cleared, of course, the boys went to the woods to work, you know.

segments.speaker: Karen Purtee
segments.words: But your father stayed and farmed?

segments.speaker: Hilda Carlson Ruberg or Helena Carlson
segments.words: Oh, yeah, he stayed and farmed. My mother died in 22. And so he farmed a couple years afterwards.

segments.speaker: Karen Purtee
segments.words: Okay, well, what type of duties did you have when you went to Spokane and became a housekeeper?

segments.speaker: Hilda Carlson Ruberg or Helena Carlson
segments.words: Oh, we just did the regular housework, you know. We did the cooking and kept the house up.

segments.speaker: Karen Purtee
segments.words: The whole thing?

segments.speaker: Hilda Carlson Ruberg or Helena Carlson
segments.words: Yeah. Yeah, we always had Thursday afternoon off to go to town. Oh, nice.

segments.speaker: Karen Purtee
segments.words: Did they give you Sunday off, too, or just Thursday?

segments.speaker: Hilda Carlson Ruberg or Helena Carlson
segments.words: Well, sometimes we had Sunday off. Sometimes we had to be there, they had company, you know. We had to cook, but we could have Sunday afternoon off, too.

segments.speaker: Karen Purtee
segments.words: And they had a place for you to live, or?

segments.speaker: Hilda Carlson Ruberg or Helena Carlson
segments.words: Oh, yeah, we lived right in the house. Yeah, it was all kind of fun, you know.

segments.speaker: Karen Purtee
segments.words: Did you work for more than one, or just one the entire time?

segments.speaker: Hilda Carlson Ruberg or Helena Carlson
segments.words: No, it was one most of the entire time. I started out at one place, you know. And, oh, I liked it there, but I didn't like it as well. I thought as I could, you know, but the back door neighbor wanted me over there. Oh. So she had a girl, you know, working for her, and she was leaving, and she wanted me to come over there to work for her, so I did that. Yeah, they were awful nice to me. Oh, they were good to me.

segments.speaker: Karen Purtee
segments.words: How'd you meet your man?

segments.speaker: Hilda Carlson Ruberg or Helena Carlson
segments.words: How'd I meet my man? Oh, my, I was at a dance hall. Oh. Yeah, wasn't that funny? And he happened to have Troy relatives, I didn't know that on the map.

segments.speaker: Karen Purtee
segments.words: Well, is that one of the things you did on your Thursday afternoon off, then, was to go dancing?

segments.speaker: Hilda Carlson Ruberg or Helena Carlson
segments.words: No, we went to, yeah, Thursday evenings, because we'd had the whole afternoon off, see? Yeah, Thursday evenings that we'd go to dances. And then there were several girls from Troy working up there, we all met downtown, and Stephen went to the dance hall. Oh. Her mother's bragged about it, she said, Hilda got the best man in the whole country, and Mabel got the second best… that's nice.

segments.speaker: Karen Purtee
segments.words: Did you have a lot of responsibility at home because you were the oldest girl? Did you have to do more than that?

segments.speaker: Hilda Carlson Ruberg or Helena Carlson
segments.words: Oh, yes, I had to do more than that, because the others that was younger than me, if anybody needed, neighbors needed any help, they always went to help the neighbors, you know, but I was always the one at home. Yeah, because I had to take care of the little kids and did the cooking and helped her out, you know. My mother always did so much outside work, too, you know.

segments.speaker: Karen Purtee
segments.words: Oh, did she?

segments.speaker: Hilda Carlson Ruberg or Helena Carlson
segments.words: Well, you know, we'd milk a lot of cows and so on, had big gardens and all that, and she was outside working. And I had to help on the inside. And you helped outside. Yeah. Oh, we were all busy all the time.

segments.speaker: Karen Purtee
segments.words: Do you have any idea how your father found out about this part of the country?

segments.speaker: Hilda Carlson Ruberg or Helena Carlson
segments.words: Well, he just thought he wanted to go out west, and he went to Oregon first. He went to Burns, Oregon, and you'd heard about that country, but he got out there and saw them rounding up jackrabbits. He got out of there. And so he came to Moscow, and he came down to Troy, and he met Mr. Duffy. This place belonged to Mr. Duffy. And so he just decided he couldn't go back home without buying something, see. Oh! He thought that he had to have something, you know, we were going to be disappointed to come back, you know. And he really, he just paid so much down, you know, because he thought he wasn't going to keep. And he came back, and Mother was so happy about it, you know. And so when the time come to go, he didn't want to go, and she says we were going. And she liked it so well out here. She was from Norway, and she said it just reminded her of Norway.

segments.speaker: Karen Purtee
segments.words: All the green trees?

segments.speaker: Hilda Carlson Ruberg or Helena Carlson
segments.words: Yeah, all the green trees and everything like that. And then there were a lot of other Norway people here, too. Yeah, a lot of Scandinavians around here. So, oh, they learned to like it, though. He learned to like it, too, but it was a lot of hard work for him, you know. He was used to farming. He wasn't used to the sawing of timber. I love you, then.

segments.speaker: Karen Purtee
segments.words: Your brother mentioned that you had a little sister that died when she was five.

segments.speaker: Hilda Carlson Ruberg or Helena Carlson
segments.words: Yeah, she died, I think she was only four. She died in 22.

segments.speaker: Karen Purtee
segments.words: The same year as your mother?

segments.speaker: Hilda Carlson Ruberg or Helena Carlson
segments.words: No, my mother died in 23. I thought my mother died in 23. No, Fern died in 1918. I said, my mother died in 22. Yeah, she was born in 1914. She was born after we came out here. Oh. Yeah, and she got burned, you know. Yeah, she had, just the day before, on Sunday, this was on Sunday, we'd all had a reunion the first time. The whole family had all been together at one time. My brother was in the Navy, and he was home, and of course my sister worked in Spokane, and Mabel and my other sister lived over in Montana. And we all got together, went down to Troy and had our picture taken on Monday. And the next morning, of course, my brother in the Navy had gone, took the train that evening, and went back to the East Coast. And the next morning, while my sister and my mother were upstairs making bids, and then Fern just got out of bed. She just woke up and went downstairs, you know, and of course they stayed upstairs. And as she went downstairs, where she went on out to the front porch and was playing with a dog out there, and on her way out she picked up some matches, I guess. And it was lighting matches on the front porch. And I guess the head flew off of the match, you know, in her nightgown. And they heard her screaming, and they ran down there and she couldn't get in the front door because it was hooked. She had to run clear around the house, and the flames was just up above her head, you know, and they pulled her nightgown off something or other, but she died a couple days after.

segments.speaker: Hilda Carlson Ruberg or Helena Carlson
segments.words: Hmm.

segments.speaker: Karen Purtee
segments.words: What did they do for people then, who were burnt?

segments.speaker: Hilda Carlson Ruberg or Helena Carlson
segments.words: Well, there wasn't no doctor in town, and they phoned to Moscow, but I guess it just happened that a doctor happened to come through town, was going to locate here, and somebody said there was a doctor in town. So he came out there, and I didn't know he couldn't do very much for her. And she was so badly burned, all around her body here, and her hair was cinched, her eyebrows cinched off, and her lips were burned, you know. I think that he said that it was, it was burned so deep, you know, it absorbed poisons inside her or something. Oh, what a beautiful thing. When she lived, about two days. Yeah, this happened Tuesday morning, and she died Wednesday evening. She was such a cutie. Yeah, I remember seeing the picture.

segments.speaker: Karen Purtee
segments.words: It must have been hard on your mother.

segments.speaker: Hilda Carlson Ruberg or Helena Carlson
segments.words: Oh, it was. It was awful hard on her.

segments.speaker: Karen Purtee
segments.words: Because I know, I've heard some people say, you know, well, half their children lived because of the different problems that they had with all the diseases, you know, but she had all her children.

segments.speaker: Hilda Carlson Ruberg or Helena Carlson
segments.words: Yeah, and they only lived for quite a while too, you know. I believe, didn't they say your family, all those children, and never one had a broken bone? Yeah, uh-huh. Until you broke yours.

segments.speaker: Karen Purtee
segments.words: Oh my goodness, that comes from good living, huh?

segments.speaker: Hilda Carlson Ruberg or Helena Carlson
segments.words: They did wild things, like climbing up on the, that was in Dakota that they climbed up on the windmills. Oh yeah, I was up there too, couldn't get down.

segments.speaker: Karen Purtee
segments.words: Really?

segments.speaker: Hilda Carlson Ruberg or Helena Carlson
segments.words: She has a broken finger to prove it. Oh yeah, that is, yeah, they had that cut off in the windmill. Oh no! Yeah, but the time they got up on the roof, of course, her mother wasn't home, seeing, of course, her daddy was working in the field. And her brother climbed up, it was kind of a house under the windmill, see, because the ground feed was the windmill too, and that feed bin, grinder was down under the, and when you climbed up the walls to get up the windmill, and of course the ... came this way and you had to get out over this, you know, and get up, and so Ed went clear up to the top of the windmill, I didn't, I sat on the roof. But when it came down to come get down, you know, I couldn't get down, I couldn't get over the ... of the roof, so I was sitting there crying until my mother came over.

segments.speaker: Hilda Carlson Ruberg or Helena Carlson
segments.words: So she got me down and gave me a whipping. Yeah, she wasn't too happy about that. You think you learned your lesson just from being up there. Well was it when you were up on there that you got your... No, that was afterwards, this was where the windmill hooked up to the pump, you know, the windmill was idling, it wasn't hooked up to the pump. And of course, you know, there's a hole where you stick the bolt in to hook it, so Ed would put his finger in the hole, and when it got to the hole where it went through, he'd pull it out and he'd go up this way, you know, come down, and I couldn't do it, and I didn't pull my hand out, and my finger went through the hole and cut it off. Oh!

segments.speaker: Karen Purtee
segments.words: Sounds to me like Ed was a little devil.

segments.speaker: Hilda Carlson Ruberg or Helena Carlson
segments.words: Oh, teaches you all these good things. ... Oh, he did have fun. I was reading that letter that you wrote to him, you know, about taking the horse, taking him home, and I'd forgotten the names of the people, the girl that had the buggy, and was going to give you a ride. Oh yeah, that was Mamie Dunn.

segments.speaker: Karen Purtee
segments.words: Well what's that all about?

segments.speaker: Hilda Carlson Ruberg or Helena Carlson
segments.words: Oh, that was... the teacher had spanked me for something that I didn't do. And we were just getting ready to go home from school, and this...

segments.speaker: Karen Purtee
segments.words: Belle Thomas was jealous that Mamie Dunn was going to take us home, see? So she went up and told the teacher, the teacher was her aunt, see?

segments.speaker: Hilda Carlson Ruberg or Helena Carlson
segments.words: And she said that Mamie's going to take Hilda and Eddie home. And she said, no, Mamie's got to go home, and Hilda and Eddie's got to walk home. And she came down and told me that, and so I just asked her, Belle, I said, well I guess if Mamie wants to take me home, we were only six years old, you know. If Mamie wants to take me home, well I guess she can, you know, and Belle went up and told the teacher that I called her an old fat sausage box. And my wife, they couldn't say anything like that, so the teacher came down behind the barn there, you know, and got me to put her across her lap, you know, and spanked me. And so she said Mamie had to go home, so I run all the way home across the fields, and they took Ed home, but they let him off about a quarter of a mile from home, you know, and the teacher, see. And I got home before Ed, and I run all the way, and so, and he told her too, you know, what happened, so Mama got mad, and she hitched up the horse, and Buggy went over and told the teacher off.

segments.speaker: Hilda Carlson Ruberg or Helena Carlson
segments.words: I'd like to do that, I'd like to do that though, because that was just the one, that's the only spanking I ever got. You didn't deserve that one. I didn't deserve that one. The other girl really deserved it for telling a lie. There's a lot of things that jealousy will do to little kids.

segments.speaker: Karen Purtee
segments.words: You'd finished school then, by the time you came out here.

segments.speaker: Hilda Carlson Ruberg or Helena Carlson
segments.words: Oh yeah, of course I never went any further than eighth grade, you know. Well that's pretty good. In those days.

segments.speaker: Karen Purtee
segments.words: In those days, that was good, wasn't it?

segments.speaker: Hilda Carlson Ruberg or Helena Carlson
segments.words: Oh yeah, in two months, it's all in. Yeah, when we first started school, we only had two months a year, you know, when we first started. And I think we only went to a nine month school about one year, you know, and then we went to seven months from two months, you know, when we first met. I remember in that letter you was telling that it only had two months of school. Yeah, uh-huh, it's in Sunday night.

segments.speaker: Karen Purtee
segments.words: Was that because of the weather in Dakota's?

segments.speaker: Hilda Carlson Ruberg or Helena Carlson
segments.words: I don't know why, I don't know why it was. That's what they used to say about Dakota. So people ask if you've stayed in Dakota, and they said, yes, so how long were you there? Uh, two winters this summer. Yeah. The weather was so violent during the winter, they had regular blizzards, you see, and just blew across and people couldn't travel. Did you remember that? Oh yeah, I know when we drove to school, you know, we had three miles at that time, and we drove, you know, in a cutter and a couple of horses. So there was a lot of snow. And it just blew right, and blew all, even, Dad said, covered the fences and everything, so you couldn't even see that there was a fence. And they drove right on top of it. Yeah, and there wasn't very many fences there where we lived, you know, nobody fenced in their fields, so if you came to a big snow drift or something, you could kind of drive around it, you know, because there was no fences to stop you. No fences to stop the snow. But I know I saw snow drifts high right in our barnyard, you know, that was ten feet high that we used to coast down.

segments.speaker: Karen Purtee
segments.words: Golly, that's a lot of snow.

segments.speaker: Hilda Carlson Ruberg or Helena Carlson
segments.words: And it was, one year it was, the snow was so deep that it drifted around the house, you couldn't see out the windows, and they had to climb up the back to get out, you know, to get to the barn to do the chores, and they finally cut a tunnel to the barn, you know, so they get down and do chores. Ah, no wonder you came to Troy. Yeah, there was a lot of snow here too, but then it didn't drift. Yeah, they didn't have the wind then. The first year we were out here, wasn't it, that first winter, they had six feet on the level? Yeah, uh-huh, six feet, and it was just beautiful. The snow would be about that high on top of each fence post, you know, and we said it looked just like a Christmas card, you know, the trees and everything, it was just beautiful. A tunnel then, just for fun. Yeah. But I don't know, then that was the spring too, I guess, either that spring, it must have been when it started melting that we had the crust on the snow, and everybody had so much fun on the crust because they could coast right over the snow.

segments.speaker: Karen Purtee
segments.words: Ah, walk on it?

segments.speaker: Hilda Carlson Ruberg or Helena Carlson
segments.words: Walk on it. I remember when Al and I first discovered that that was our first experience with crust, we went out there and very carefully, you know, and then we got in on our stomachs and crawled around, we did great. Finally we tried it by walking, and then we just discovered we could run on it, and boy, we were like a couple of fairies standing in the snow, and it was moonlight too, it was beautiful. We were out there sailing around, we got so excited, we could walk on the snow, it was fun.

segments.speaker: Karen Purtee
segments.words: Is that what they call the silver thaw or the silver crust?

segments.speaker: Hilda Carlson Ruberg or Helena Carlson
segments.words: Silver thaw, I guess. Yeah, I suppose it had rained, I think another, the snow had settled by that time enough, you see, sort of packed, and then frozen, so it was really quite exciting. Our experience.

segments.speaker: Karen Purtee
segments.words: We have a piece of that, what is it? Fattigmann? Fattigmann?

segments.speaker: Hilda Carlson Ruberg or Helena Carlson
segments.words: Yeah, it went down your throat. Yep. Sort of. Here we go.

segments.speaker: Karen Purtee
segments.words: Did your mother have all her children at home, or with a doctor, or midwife?

segments.speaker: Hilda Carlson Ruberg or Helena Carlson
segments.words: Yeah, no, they were all born at home. All at home.

segments.speaker: Karen Purtee
segments.words: Did she have doctors come, or did?

segments.speaker: Hilda Carlson Ruberg or Helena Carlson
segments.words: Sometimes, and sometimes not.

segments.speaker: Karen Purtee
segments.words: Just, depended on if he was around, huh?

segments.speaker: Hilda Carlson Ruberg or Helena Carlson
segments.words: Yeah, well, it's, I know she had the doctor for Alice in France, you know, but for the others, I can't remember, but they were all born at home, but they had somebody come in, you know, some woman come in.

segments.speaker: Karen Purtee
segments.words: You weren't old enough when the last ones came along, did you help her?

segments.speaker: Hilda Carlson Ruberg or Helena Carlson
segments.words: No, no.

segments.speaker: Karen Purtee
segments.words: What did she do with the rest of your kids when she was going to have a baby?

segments.speaker: Hilda Carlson Ruberg or Helena Carlson
segments.words: We were all home… were you… oh, yeah. I remember when Hester was born, we were invited to go up and visit grandmother. Oh. So we weren't at home, you know, at the time. Ed's brother was the doctor. They didn't live too far from us, so he was down there. I remember Alba and I said, we bet you we know what's going to happen. We bet they're going to have a baby. Oh. But they didn't tell you. You just had to guess it. They hadn't told a word, you know. In those days, they didn't tell people like they do now. No, uh-uh. Now the kids know all about it. They know all about it. Yeah. From the beginning, but not when we were growing up. We didn't know anything.

segments.speaker: Karen Purtee
segments.words: Did you notice that there was something different about your mother?

segments.speaker: Hilda Carlson Ruberg or Helena Carlson
segments.words: I can't remember that I did. No, I can't remember that we did either. No, didn't make any impression. We saw the cows and the pigs and the cats, but we never thought too much about that either, and we definitely never thought about mother.

segments.speaker: Karen Purtee
segments.words: What was the explanation for the new baby in the house?

segments.speaker: Hilda Carlson Ruberg or Helena Carlson
segments.words: Well, I can't remember. I remember when Bill was born, you know, and one of the neighbor women was over there, you know, and so they said that they found him in a hawks nest. I can't remember. We were so gullible, I guess, that we didn't really need any explanation. I guess they just said they had a baby sister for us, but in a way, in our little minds, we kind of had a feeling. We knew where the baby had come from, but we never talked it over with the folks, and they never talked it over with us, but my sister and I, we kind of talked it over between ourselves, you know, and I remember that we were just little kids, and I think it was after that, or no, it was before that, because we were younger, and I remember, she said, you know, I think I'm going to have a baby. I said, you do? And she thought she was, and here she was, years old.

segments.speaker: Karen Purtee
segments.words: How old?

segments.speaker: Hilda Carlson Ruberg or Helena Carlson
segments.words: Oh, she must have been five, six years old. Oh, yeah.

segments.speaker: Karen Purtee
segments.words: What made her think she was going to have a baby?

segments.speaker: Hilda Carlson Ruberg or Helena Carlson
segments.words: I don't know why she thought so. But she said, you know, I kind of think I'm going to have a baby. That was kind of an interesting sensation. Oh, yeah. The baby never progressed. Oh, not at that age. But we did, I suppose we had kind of an idea about things, because my dad always had cows, you see, and he ran the bull with the cows, and we saw a lot of carrying on like that, but I really don't know, to begin with, even that didn't make any impression particularly, only that after a while, behold, they began to have cows, you know, and I suppose in our stupid little minds, why there's something, there might have been a sort of connection that made finally that there was something. But you never sat down and explained things. No, never. We weren't there… never either.

segments.speaker: Karen Purtee
segments.words: What about as a girl matured, when the facts of life became necessary?

segments.speaker: Hilda Carlson Ruberg or Helena Carlson
segments.words: No, we never told about that either. You just got a surprise from that. Yeah, uh-huh, yeah. My mother gave me a little pamphlet to read one time. That was the only thing that was ever said about that time, you know, and she was on the watch, you know, and I remember when it first happened, why I was scared to death. I had eaten beets that day. And I... That was what it was, and I remember hiding in my closet, you know, and I was wondering what on earth to do. I was worrying about it and everything, like, why, I sure took those beets. Never eat beets again. Never again. Then I guess my mother knew that there was something she was watching. So then she said, well, I'm prepared, but you just expect that, she said. And then she told me probably how often it would be and everything. That was my information.

segments.speaker: Hilda Carlson Ruberg or Helena Carlson
segments.words: Just like that, okay. Because now they have movies and books. Yeah. Yeah, and even... The boys get the information just like the girls, you know. Uh-huh, and then they even had... I understand, I didn't see that, but they even showed a birth on the TV from beginning to end, and I don't know if they showed it to the kids or not. I never... Yeah, they showed it at seven o 'clock at night, and I sat down and my daughter watched it. You did. Watched it together. Well, I know, I don't remember, I must have been... It was after we'd come to Troy. I never did watch a birth, even of a kitten, and I was too embarrassed to watch that. I came in the house one day, and there was some other cat. segments.words: Ed, yeah, he was about 22 when Fern was born because he was 20 when he came out here and she was born two years afterwards. Yeah. So they had plenty of help. Bigger ones. That doesn't make it feel quite so bad. Well, Fern was born when we were working in Spokane, you know, we weren't home.

segments.speaker: Karen Purtee
segments.words: Did you know that there was another one on the way?

segments.speaker: Hilda Carlson Ruberg or Helena Carlson
segments.words: Oh, yeah… she never mentioned it to us, but we could tell, of course. Yeah, by then. Yeah, we thought, my goodness, another one, you know. Yeah, in fact, she thought she had a tumor and she told it in front of the crowds, you know, that she had a tumor and was going to have to have an operation. Pretty soon she kept talking about it. Mother wondered how come and then the tumor arrived. Oh, I never heard about that. No, I never heard about that. Yeah, she would tell us, you know, that she had a tumor and she guessed she was going to have to have an operation. And in mixed crowds she was talking about, you know, she was going to have to have an operation for this tumor. And all of a sudden, nothing, we heard nothing more about the tumor and I remember Mother's wondering about that.
